rv.q: This classic Cold War farce feels more timely and more terrifying than ever.
Perhaps it’s that framework that makes this something of a hit-and-miss evening.

This production achieves the dubious feat of turning an edgy, absurdist story into broad entertainment with accessible laughs, along with a few topical references and excellent performances all round.
It’s a lovable but overly reverential approach to a film classic that’s sturdy enough to withstand a braver spin.

It also made you wish the show’s co-adaptors, Armando Iannucci and Sean Foley, had applied a few more creative flourishes to what is, all in all, a stolid remake of the classic Stanley Kubrick Cold War satire.
It’s an accomplished, funny West End comedy, and even if the Cold War is over it still has some topical bite.
Sean Foley, alas, is no Stanley Kubrick.
It’s a question the show never adequately answers, trapped between the film’s formidable legacy and an inability to recreate it anew theatrically.
That’s what all but the most disciplined of the audience will be doing (except those who are using Alan Partridge as the comparator) and something that the production leans into with its sets.

Film director Stanley Kubrick’s savage and irreverent 1964 black comedy Dr Strangelove Or: How I Learned To The Bomb, tapped into the creeping paranoia of the Cold War and has become a timeless movie parody.
This is then – rather like Dr Strangelove with his rebellious prosthetic limbs – an evening of different parts, some functioning better than others.
It’s entertaining but never quite as savage as you expect.
But just as how the movie stood as a testament to Sellers’ talent, this new play is an absolute shrine to Coogan’s. There is barely a moment where he isn’t on stage in one or other of his characters.

The fourth and final is the titular character, Dr. While we’re in for a wait to see this character for the first time, it is more than worth it as Coogan delivers a true masterclass performance with perfect comedic execution in a wickedly funny characterisation.

J.C, LondonLivingLarge: There is a great deal of silliness and some very funny running gags, and if possible, the characters seem even more exaggerated than in the original. Steve Coogan takes on the multiple roles played by the unforgettable Peter Sellers (Dr.

In an ash blonde wig and scooting around in a wheelchair, Coogan’s Strangelove is faithful to the Wernher von Braun-like character without replicating Sellers’ performance. As the bewildered British officer Captain Mandrake he is vocally a dead ringer for King Charles III which adds to the fun.
